high.title: Brazil Set to Be First Target of New Round of Trump Tariffs; 25% Rate Could Hit 4,000 Products
high.summary: Brazil is bracing for the imposition of a new 25% tariff by the United States, potentially affecting more than 4,000 Brazilian export products. According to four sources cited by Reuters who have been tracking negotiations, Brazil is expected to be the **first target** in a new wave of US tariff actions against multiple countries — this following the US Supreme Court's invalidation of the Trump administration's original tariff framework. Months of negotiations between Brasília and Washington have yielded little progress.

high.title: Market Reacts to New US Tariff Shock Against Brazil; Ibovespa in Dollar Terms Falls Today (16)
high.summary:
The Brazilian market is absorbing the impact of the US decision to impose an additional 25% tariff on Brazilian products, effective July 22, as the Ibovespa measured in USD terms declines on the day. The tariff was formalized under Section 301 of the US Trade Act of 1974 following a USTR investigation. Critically, the article notes that the effective impact may be partially cushioned by an extensive exceptions list — over 2,000 products were exempted from the surcharge, including key Brazilian export items such as beef. For FX traders, this is a material BRL-negative development: reduced export revenue prospects weaken Brazil's trade surplus dynamics and diminish USD inflows, putting upward pressure on USD/BRL. Bond investors should monitor whether the tariff shock feeds through to inflation (via a weaker Real) or dampens growth expectations — both of which have implications for COPOM's rate trajectory. The Ibovespa's dollar-denominated decline signals foreign investor risk-off sentiment toward Brazilian assets. Watch the Real's reaction closely into July 22, when the tariffs take effect.

medium.title: Markets Monitor Weaker Inflation and Ormuz Tensions; Ibovespa in Dollar Terms Falls Today (15)
medium.summary: International markets are operating cautiously amid persistent Middle East geopolitical tensions, with President Trump walking back a proposed 20% transit fee on vessels crossing the Strait of Hormuz in favor of Gulf investment cooperation agreements. Despite this de-escalation, the regional situation remains fragile. The **Ibovespa measured in USD terms declined** on the session, reflecting a combination of BRL weakness and equity softness. The backdrop of weaker-than-expected US inflation data is providing some risk appetite globally but has not been sufficient to lift Brazilian assets. For BRL and Ibovespa traders, the interplay between global risk sentiment, commodity price dynamics (particularly oil via Ormuz), and the evolving US tariff narrative remains the central focus in the near term.

medium.title: BTG Sees Another Difficult Quarter for Brazilian Retail; High Interest Rates and Elevated Household Debt Weigh
medium.summary: BTG Pactual's research desk expects Q2 2026 to mark yet another challenging quarter for Brazilian retail companies, with no meaningful improvement in the macro environment for consumers. Persistently **high Selic rate levels** continue to erode disposable income, while elevated household indebtedness and cumulative inflation keep purchasing power suppressed. This note has indirect but relevant macro implications: it underscores that **monetary policy transmission remains tight**, validating a restrictive BCB stance, and signals that domestic consumption-driven equity plays face continued earnings pressure. Ibovespa investors should note that consumer discretionary and retail segments remain structurally challenged in the current rate environment.

medium.title: Trump Tariff Threatens US$11 Billion in Brazilian Exports, Says Amcham
medium.summary:
The American Chamber of Commerce for Brazil (Amcham Brasil) characterized the US decision to impose a 25% additional tariff on approximately 3,000 Brazilian products as a "very negative" outcome for the bilateral trade relationship. The measure, formalized on July 15 under Section 301 of the US Trade Act of 1974, takes effect on July 22. Amcham's quantification of US$11 billion in threatened export revenue provides a concrete macro anchor for market participants — this figure represents meaningful pressure on Brazil's current account and trade balance, which are key supports for the BRL. While exceptions to the tariff list may soften the headline impact (as noted in Article 2), the scale of the threat warrants monitoring for downstream effects on Brazil's fiscal revenues, export-linked equities (particularly in agribusiness and commodities), and ultimately the BCB's assessment of external sector risks in future COPOM communications.
